plan.chapterName: OpenStax Calculus, chapter 14: Differentiation of Functions of Several Variables
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a three-dimensional diagram pairing a shaded surface with a set of direction arrows and their projections onto the plane below. An upward-opening paraboloid, shaded cream at the left, blue across the right rim, and orange along its lower flank, is drawn with the z-axis rising through it, the y-axis running to the right, and the x-axis coming forward at the lower left. A black dot on the near face of the bowl is labeled P0 (x0, y0, z0) by a leader line to the right. Three kinds of arrows leave that dot: an orange one angling up and to the right along the steepest rise, a dark blue one angling down and to the left, and a pair of teal arrows lying along a teal curve that wraps horizontally around the bowl at constant height. Red and gray dashed drop lines carry the arrangement down to a small flat copy of itself on the plane, where the blue arrow is labeled minus grad f with the note Most rapid decrease in f, the orange arrow is labeled grad f with Most rapid increase in f, and the teal arrows are labeled Zero change in f, and a small square marks the right angle between the gradient direction and the level direction. Flattening the three directions into the plane is what makes that perpendicularity visible. The diagram illustrates how the directional derivative reaches its largest value along the gradient, its most negative value opposite the gradient, and zero along the level curve.

elements: upward-opening paraboloid bowl z = (x² + y²)/4, shaded cream on the left, blue across the right rim, orange along the lower flank
z-axis vertical through the bowl center with arrowhead, labeled z
y-axis running to the right with arrowhead, labeled y
x-axis coming forward to the lower left with arrowhead, labeled x
black dot P0 on the near face of the bowl, with leader line to label 'P0 (x0, y0, z0)' on the right
orange arrow from P0 angling up and to the right along the steepest ascent direction (tangent to surface)
dark blue arrow from P0 angling down and to the left along the steepest descent direction
teal level curve wrapping horizontally around the bowl at constant height z0 through P0
pair of teal arrows tangent to the level curve at P0 (both senses of the level direction)
red dashed vertical drop lines from P0 and from the arrow tips down to the plane diagram

small flat projected diagram below the bowl: projected black dot, projected blue arrow labeled −∇f, projected orange arrow labeled ∇f, projected teal arrows, small square right-angle marker between the gradient direction and the level direction
labels: 'Most rapid decrease in f' (beside −∇f), 'Most rapid increase in f' (beside ∇f), 'Zero change in f' (beside teal arrows)

interactions.label: Direction angle θ at P0
interactions.teaches: Rotating the direction arrow around P0 sweeps the directional derivative D_u f = |∇f|cosθ through its maximum along ∇f, through zero along the level direction, to its minimum along −∇f — alignment with the gradient is what controls the rate of change

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Flattening the 3D arrows into the plane projection reveals the right angle between ∇f and the level direction — perpendicularity that is hard to read on the curved surface
Hovering ∇f, −∇f, or the teal level direction highlights the matching surface arrow and its label, distinguishing maximum increase, maximum decrease, and zero change at P0

demo_steps.title: Steepest ascent
demo_steps.narration: θ = 0° aligns the direction arrow with ∇f: the directional derivative equals |∇f|, its maximum. The orange arrow and 'Most rapid increase' label highlight.

demo_steps.title: Zero change
demo_steps.narration: θ = 90° points along the level curve: D_u f = 0. In the plane projection the right-angle marker shows the direction is exactly perpendicular to ∇f.

demo_steps.title: Steepest descent
demo_steps.narration: θ = 180° opposes the gradient: D_u f = −|∇f|, the most rapid decrease. The blue arrow highlights on both the surface and the projected diagram.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Paraboloid z = (x²+y²)/4 spanning x,y ∈ [-2.5, 2.5], so rim height ≈ 3.1 world units; bowl drawn as open surface (no top cap), rim at the top, vertex at origin-ish. Gradient colors: cream #f5f0dc left/upper-left, blue #7fa8d0 across right rim, orange #e8703a along lower flank. P0 sits on the near face at roughly (1.2, 1.6, 1.0); ∇f direction at P0 is (2x0, 2y0)/4 = (0.6, 0.8) in the xy-plane (normalize for arrow); arrow length ~1.0. Orange arrow #e8703a up-right (steep ascent), dark blue arrow #1a3a6b down-left (opposite), teal arrows #1f9e8e tangent to the level circle x²+y² = x0²+y0² at height z0 = 1.0 (level curve drawn as teal circle of radius ~2.0 at z = 1.0). Red dashed vertical lines from P0 and arrow tips down to z = -2.2 where the flat projected diagram lives: projected dot, ∇f arrow (orange), −∇f (blue), teal level direction pair, and a small square right-angle marker at the projected dot. z-axis up through bowl center, y-axis to the right, x-axis toward lower-left, all black with arrowheads, spanning ~±4 units. Directional derivative readout: D_u f = |∇f| cos θ with |∇f| = 1.0 after normalization.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the paraboloid as a ParametricGeometry with vertex-color gradient (cream→blue by angle around z, orange band near the bottom flank). The rotating direction arrow from the slider should be drawn twice coherently: once tangent-projected on the surface near P0 and once in the flat projected diagram; in 'Plane projection' view, fade the bowl (opacity ~0.15) and emphasize the flat diagram with the right-angle marker. Show a live numeric readout of D_u f = cos θ. Hover on labels/arrows toggles emissive highlight on the matching arrow pair (surface + projection) and dims the other two.

authoredContext:
Suppose the function z=f(x,y) is differentiable at (x0,y0) (the figure).

The ‖u‖ disappears because u is a unit vector. Therefore, the directional derivative is equal to the magnitude of the gradient evaluated at (x0,y0) multiplied by cosφ. Recall that cosφ ranges from −1 to 1. If φ=0, then cosφ=1 and ∇f(x0,y0) and u both point in the same direction. If φ=π, then cosφ=−1 and ∇f(x0,y0) and u point in opposite directions. In the first case, the value of Duf(x0,y0) is maximized; in the second case, the value of Duf(x0,y0) is minimized. If ∇f(x0,y0)=0, then Duf(x0,y0)=∇f(x0,y0)·u=0 for any vector u. These three cases are outlined in the following theorem.

The gradient indicates the maximum and minimum values of the directional derivative at a point.

An upward facing paraboloid in xyz space with point P0 (x0, y0, z0). From this point, there are arrows going up, down, and around the paraboloid. On the xy plane, the point (x0, y0) is marked, and the corresponding arrows are drawn onto the plane: the down arrow corresponds to −∇f (most rapid decrease in f), the up arrow corresponds to ∇f (most rapid increase in f), and the arrows around correspond to no change in f. The up/down arrows are perpendicular to the around arrows in their projection on the plane.

The figure shows a portion of the graph of the function f(x,y)=3+sinxsiny. Given a point (a,b) in the domain of f, the maximum value of the gradient at that point is given by ‖∇f(a,b)‖. This would equal the rate of greatest ascent if the surface represented a topographical map. If we went in the opposite direction, it would be the rate of greatest descent.

plan.chapterName: OpenStax Calculus, chapter 14: Differentiation of Functions of Several Variables
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a three-dimensional diagram pairing a shaded surface with a set of direction arrows and their projections onto the plane below. An upward-opening paraboloid, shaded cream at the left, blue across the right rim, and orange along its lower flank, is drawn with the z-axis rising through it, the y-axis running to the right, and the x-axis coming forward at the lower left. A black dot on the near face of the bowl is labeled P0 (x0, y0, z0) by a leader line to the right. Three kinds of arrows leave that dot: an orange one angling up and to the right along the steepest rise, a dark blue one angling down and to the left, and a pair of teal arrows lying along a teal curve that wraps horizontally around the bowl at constant height. Red and gray dashed drop lines carry the arrangement down to a small flat copy of itself on the plane, where the blue arrow is labeled minus grad f with the note Most rapid decrease in f, the orange arrow is labeled grad f with Most rapid increase in f, and the teal arrows are labeled Zero change in f, and a small square marks the right angle between the gradient direction and the level direction. Flattening the three directions into the plane is what makes that perpendicularity visible. The diagram illustrates how the directional derivative reaches its largest value along the gradient, its most negative value opposite the gradient, and zero along the level curve.

elements: upward-opening paraboloid bowl z = (x² + y²)/4, shaded cream on the left, blue across the right rim, orange along the lower flank
z-axis vertical through the bowl center with arrowhead, labeled z
y-axis running to the right with arrowhead, labeled y
x-axis coming forward to the lower left with arrowhead, labeled x
black dot P0 on the near face of the bowl, with leader line to label 'P0 (x0, y0, z0)' on the right
orange arrow from P0 angling up and to the right along the steepest ascent direction (tangent to surface)
dark blue arrow from P0 angling down and to the left along the steepest descent direction
teal level curve wrapping horizontally around the bowl at constant height z0 through P0
pair of teal arrows tangent to the level curve at P0 (both senses of the level direction)

labels: 'Most rapid decrease in f' (beside −∇f), 'Most rapid increase in f' (beside ∇f), 'Zero change in f' (beside teal arrows)

interactions.label: Direction angle θ at P0
interactions.teaches: Rotating the direction arrow around P0 sweeps the directional derivative D_u f = |∇f|cosθ through its maximum along ∇f, through zero along the level direction, to its minimum along −∇f — alignment with the gradient is what controls the rate of change

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Flattening the 3D arrows into the plane projection reveals the right angle between ∇f and the level direction — perpendicularity that is hard to read on the curved surface
Hovering ∇f, −∇f, or the teal level direction highlights the matching surface arrow and its label, distinguishing maximum increase, maximum decrease, and zero change at P0

demo_steps.title: Steepest ascent
demo_steps.narration: θ = 0° aligns the direction arrow with ∇f: the directional derivative equals |∇f|, its maximum. The orange arrow and 'Most rapid increase' label highlight.

demo_steps.title: Zero change
demo_steps.narration: θ = 90° points along the level curve: D_u f = 0. In the plane projection the right-angle marker shows the direction is exactly perpendicular to ∇f.

demo_steps.title: Steepest descent
demo_steps.narration: θ = 180° opposes the gradient: D_u f = −|∇f|, the most rapid decrease. The blue arrow highlights on both the surface and the projected diagram.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Paraboloid z = (x²+y²)/4 spanning x,y ∈ [-2.5, 2.5], so rim height ≈ 3.1 world units; bowl drawn as open surface (no top cap), rim at the top, vertex at origin-ish. Gradient colors: cream #f5f0dc left/upper-left, blue #7fa8d0 across right rim, orange #e8703a along lower flank. P0 sits on the near face at roughly (1.2, 1.6, 1.0); ∇f direction at P0 is (2x0, 2y0)/4 = (0.6, 0.8) in the xy-plane (normalize for arrow); arrow length ~1.0. Orange arrow #e8703a up-right (steep ascent), dark blue arrow #1a3a6b down-left (opposite), teal arrows #1f9e8e tangent to the level circle x²+y² = x0²+y0² at height z0 = 1.0 (level curve drawn as teal circle of radius ~2.0 at z = 1.0). Red dashed vertical lines from P0 and arrow tips down to z = -2.2 where the flat projected diagram lives: projected dot, ∇f arrow (orange), −∇f (blue), teal level direction pair, and a small square right-angle marker at the projected dot. z-axis up through bowl center, y-axis to the right, x-axis toward lower-left, all black with arrowheads, spanning ~±4 units. Directional derivative readout: D_u f = |∇f| cos θ with |∇f| = 1.0 after normalization.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the paraboloid as a ParametricGeometry with vertex-color gradient (cream→blue by angle around z, orange band near the bottom flank). The rotating direction arrow from the slider should be drawn twice coherently: once tangent-projected on the surface near P0 and once in the flat projected diagram; in 'Plane projection' view, fade the bowl (opacity ~0.15) and emphasize the flat diagram with the right-angle marker. Show a live numeric readout of D_u f = cos θ. Hover on labels/arrows toggles emissive highlight on the matching arrow pair (surface + projection) and dims the other two.
